_bands.note: A yearly cost counts ten years. The figure under each band is the range for one typical square mile.

_square_mile.text: We laid a 1-mile grid over SF's 47.1 square miles of land and dropped the cells that are under half land or over half park, open space or water (Rec and Park property or the Presidio), which leaves 42 of 66, and leaves out Golden Gate Park, the Presidio, Lake Merced, McLaren Park and Treasure Island. The typical square mile is the average of those 42, the same cells whose crashes give each tool's share: 23.1 street miles (2.9 arterial, 5.4 collector, 14.8 residential), 3.6 miles of the High Injury Network, 153 intersections (78 on a main street, 24 of them on an arterial, 75 on residential streets only), 202 residential blocks and 29 traffic signals (14 on arterials). A main street is one DataSF's centerlines class as arterial or collector, or one OpenStreetMap tags trunk, primary, secondary or tertiary. That is OpenStreetMap's judgement: Polk and Valencia count as main streets, Eddy, Irving and Clement stay residential. Each tool is counted only where it goes: main-street tools on main-street corners or miles, residential tools on residential blocks, signal tools at signals. Signals are OpenStreetMap's, since DataSF doesn't publish SFMTA's inventory. Built today compares SF's count with the square mile's quantity times 42, or with the citywide count where one exists.

_coverage_rule: Built today: the share of the places a tool fits, citywide, that have it now, counting the same places the cost column counts (for example 65% of intersections daylit); each info box names the count it is out of. Counts come from DataSF and SFMTA inventories where they exist; ~ marks our estimate, and 'no count' means none is published.
_shares_note: Effect is the change in all injury crashes across a typical square mile once the tool is built everywhere the cost column puts it, the same places the cost column prices. It is the study's effect where the tool goes, times the share of the square mile's injury crashes that happen at that kind of place (DataSF crashes 2022-2025 inside the same 42 cells the square mile averages, 11,095 of them), times the share of those places the cost column treats. Built today is a separate column and does not change the effect. Where the study counted only pedestrians, only pedestrian crashes are counted, so the figure leaves other road users unchanged. Each info box shows the arithmetic.
_skipped: Left out as rural or freeway tools: rumble strips, median barriers, SafetyEdge, wider edge lines, curve delineation, roadside design at curves and variable speed limits. Left out as suburban designs: reduced left-turn conflict intersections and corridor access management. Left out as planning processes: road safety audits and local road safety plans. Folded in: turn lanes into Removing a car lane, stop-sign sight-line work into Daylighting, chicanes into Calmed 20 mph zones, plazas and shared streets into Car-free streets, busways into Transit-only lanes, AB 43 limits into Lower speed limits, Vision Zero's painted safety zones into Bulb-outs, its new traffic signals and quick-build program into Bigger, brighter signals, and NYC's mid-block narrowing and gateways into Calmed 20 mph zones, its greenways into Bike priority slow streets, and its conventional and two-way bike lanes into Protected bike lanes. Left out as transit or sidewalk design rather than safety tools: NYC's bus bulbs and boarding islands and sidewalk expansion. Also left out: walkways, since SF streets nearly all have sidewalks, and pavement friction, which FHWA aims at curves, ramps and fast approaches (our judgement).
